title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
takeaways: A stack is the natural data structure for postfix notation evaluation as operators act on the most recently parsed operands.
Order of operands matters for non-commutative operations like subtraction and division; the first popped element is the second (right) operand.
Be cautious with integer division truncating toward zero depending on the language (e.g., Python's // truncates towards negative infinity, so int(a / b) should be used instead).
Operand/operator discrimination: every operator is exactly one character, so any token of length >= 2 must be a number. That single fact handles negative literals like -11 with no special case.
Trigger to memorise: 'evaluate an expression where operators follow their operands' -> stack, because operators consume the most recently produced values (LIFO by definition).
Parenthesise && inside || even when precedence already gives the right answer; compilers warn (-Wparentheses) because it is a common misreading.
C++ integer division truncates toward zero, guaranteed since C++11 (-7/2 == -3), which matches this problem's spec exactly.
self_assessment: Expected to need a postfix/infix tutorial first and instead derived it cold. Confirms the just-in-time theory rule: RPN evaluation passes the 'can I derive this in 25 minutes' test, so studying first would have been wasted. Calibration note: I underestimate what I can derive.
